data.title: Piebaldism — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Piebaldism** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define piebaldism.**
- Rare autosomal dominant congenital disorder of melanocyte migration/differentiation (KIT proto-oncogene loss-of-function; also SNAI2) with stable depigmented patches present from birth and a white forelock

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- White forelock (poliosis) with triangular/diamond-shaped depigmented patch on the mid-forehead in ~80–90%
- Symmetrical depigmented patches on ventral trunk, mid-extremities (sparing hands, feet and back), often with islands of normal or hyperpigmented skin inside and at margins
- Eyebrows/eyelashes may be white; lesions stable throughout life (no progression, may partially repigment)
- No systemic involvement (vs Waardenburg — deafness, heterochromia, dystopia canthorum)

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Absent or markedly reduced melanocytes in depigmented skin (confirmed by DOPA/immunostains); normal melanocytes at hyperpigmented islands

**Q4. Differentiate piebaldism from vitiligo.**
- Piebaldism: present at birth, stable, specific distribution (forehead, ventral trunk, mid-limbs), white forelock, hyperpigmented islands, family history (AD), no Koebner or progression, no autoimmune association
- Vitiligo: acquired, progressive or relapsing, any site (acral, periorificial), Koebner, autoimmune associations, responds to medical therapy

**Q5. Other differentials.**
- Waardenburg syndrome, nevus depigmentosus, Ziprkowski–Margolis (X-linked albinism–deafness), Tietz syndrome, hypomelanosis of Ito, tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf), Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (acquired poliosis)

**Q6. Management.**
- Genetic counselling (50% risk to offspring), sun protection of depigmented skin, camouflage
- Medical therapy (phototherapy) is ineffective because melanocytes are absent; surgical — suction blister grafts, mini-punch grafts, non-cultured epidermal cell suspension work well because disease is stable

**Q7. What is the white forelock and differential diagnosis of poliosis?**
- Localised patch of white hair (poliosis) — piebaldism, Waardenburg syndrome, vitiligo, alopecia areata regrowth, halo naevus, Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada, Alezzandrini syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, NF1, post-inflammatory/ radiation, Marfan (rare)

**Q8. Explain grafting outcomes in piebaldism.**
- Excellent and stable repigmentation with mini-punch grafting, suction blister grafts, non-cultured melanocyte–keratinocyte transplant because the disorder is stable and recipient sites lack inflammation; post-graft NB-UVB may enhance

**Q9. What is Woolf/ Tietz syndrome?**
- Tietz (MITF): generalised hypopigmentation (albinoid) with congenital profound deafness, AD
- Ziprkowski–Margolis (Woolf): X-linked albinism–deafness with piebald-like patches

**Q10. Is piebaldism associated with Hirschsprung disease?**
- Classic piebaldism is not; but piebaldism-like pigmentation with Hirschsprung disease suggests Waardenburg type 4 (Shah–Waardenburg — EDNRB, EDN3, SOX10) — check bowel symptoms and hearing

**Q11. What is the role of camouflage?**
- Waterproof cosmetic cover creams, dihydroxyacetone self-tanners, micropigmentation/ tattooing for small stable areas, hair dye for forelock; sunscreen for depigmented skin to prevent sunburn

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. Explain the molecular basis.**
- KIT encodes the tyrosine kinase receptor for stem cell factor; loss-of-function (dominant-negative mutations are more severe) prevents melanoblast migration from the neural crest and survival in ventral and midline areas — hence the distribution

**Q14. What is the role of SCF/KIT in other disorders?**
- Gain-of-function KIT mutations: mastocytosis (D816V), gastrointestinal stromal tumours, acral and mucosal melanomas — treated with KIT inhibitors (imatinib), whereas piebaldism is loss-of-function

**Q15. Why are hyperpigmented islands seen?**
- Melanocytes that do reach these areas can be hyperfunctional; CALM-like macules in piebaldism may cause confusion with NF1 (piebaldism with CALMs — check KIT vs NF1/SPRED1)

## Quick spotter facts
- White forelock + ventral depigmentation from birth, stable — piebaldism (KIT)
- Responds to grafting, not phototherapy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Genetic hypomelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
